questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Two weaknesses used in sequence
questions.learningObjective: Recognise when two weaknesses combine so one enables the other
questions.stem: A dispatcher's terminal accepts a ticket reference without checking the booking origin, and that ticket can then name a train to divert. What does the pair create?

options.text: A chain in which the first weakness hands over control that the second weakness then uses
A single weakness counted twice, since both entries describe the same missing check
options.misconception: treats two distinct entries as one repeated weakness

options.text: A reporting gap only, because neither entry changes what a dispatcher can do
options.misconception: believes the entries have no effect on dispatcher actions

options.text: A hardware fault, since a chained weakness must come from a failed device
options.misconception: assumes chained weaknesses must be physical faults

questions.explanation: The first weakness lets an attacker supply a reference, and the second converts that into control of a service, so the two act in sequence. Treating them as one repeated weakness is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Ask what the first one hands to the second.

options.text: The exact number of affected sites, so the reader can size the work immediately
options.misconception: assumes a category carries a count of affected sites

options.text: The fix that will be applied, so the reader can deploy it as soon as it reads
options.misconception: assumes a category contains the fix

options.text: The kind of effect the weakness has, so readers can judge where it applies
The schedule of remediation, since categories are published alongside dates
options.misconception: assumes a category includes the rollout schedule

questions.explanation: A category states the kind of effect a weakness produces, which is what lets a reader decide whether it applies to their own systems. Reading a category as a count, a fix or a schedule is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Ask what effect the category is naming.

options.misconception: believes a staying component keeps its full reachable set

options.text: A smaller reachable set, since only the permitted machines can now use it
A smaller reachable set only for the printer, with every other device unchanged
options.misconception: assumes access rules shrink one device and not the path

options.text: The same reach as before, because reach depends on the component and not on access rules
options.misconception: believes reach ignores who is permitted to connect

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Holding a risk down while the fix is pending
questions.learningObjective: Explain what holding a risk down means while a fix is pending
questions.stem: Explain what it means to hold a risk down while the permanent fix is pending, and what a supervisor checks.

answer.exemplar: A model answer explains that holding a risk down means the exposure is reduced but not removed, by cutting the path, the privilege or the lifetime of the access until the permanent fix arrives. It adds that a supervisor checks that the temporary control is still in force, that it covers every affected route rather than one instance, and that it has an owner and an end date, so that the control is not quietly dropped when the fix is delayed.

questions.explanation: Holding a risk down reduces exposure for the waiting period without pretending the weakness is gone. Treating the interim measure as a permanent fix, or as paperwork, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Reduced exposure for now, with an owner and an end date.

questions.topic: A boundary check that permits a bare parent reference

stimulus.body: The depot manifest service checks that a requested path stays inside the depot folder, but it accepts a path that is simply the parent directory name with no further path. A request that names only the parent still passes the check.

questions.stem: Given that note, what does the check actually allow?

options.text: Nothing unusual, because a parent path never contains a restricted file name
options.misconception: assumes a parent reference cannot reach any restricted file

options.text: Only a listing of the parent folder, which holds no dispatch records at all
options.misconception: assumes the parent folder is empty of anything useful

options.text: Any file inside the parent folder, since the check treats the parent as inside the depot
options.misconception: believes the check treats a parent as inside the depot tree

options.text: Access to files held one level above the intended folder, because the parent passes the test

questions.explanation: A check that accepts the parent name lets anything under that parent resolve, so files one level above the intended folder become reachable. Assuming the parent holds nothing of value, or that the check treats it as inside, is the tempting error.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a boundary check alone does not close a weakness
questions.stem: The manifest service now rejects any path that leaves the depot folder. Why is that still not enough on its own?

options.text: It removes one kind of bad path, while files reachable by other means can still be exposed
It removes every kind of bad path, so the remaining problem is only the naming of files
options.misconception: believes a boundary check removes every class of bad path

options.text: It is too strict, because rejecting every path outside the folder breaks legitimate work
options.misconception: treats a strict boundary check as the cause of broken work

options.text: It only affects reads, because writes to other folders are checked by a separate rule
options.misconception: assumes writes and reads follow separate exposure paths

questions.explanation: A boundary check answers one narrow question about a path, so it closes the most obvious route while exports, shares and copies can still deliver the same data. Believing one check closes every route, or that reads and writes differ, is the tempting error.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a boundary check is necessary but not sufficient
questions.learningObjective: Explain the necessity and the limits of a boundary check
questions.stem: Explain why a boundary check is necessary but not sufficient, using the manifest service as the example.

answer.exemplar: A model answer explains that a boundary check is necessary because without it any request can name a path outside the intended folder and read material the operator never offered, so it removes the most obvious route. It then explains the limits: the check only answers whether a path resolves inside the folder, not whether the person asking may see the record, not whether the same record is reachable by another service, an export or a share, and not whether a reference held inside the folder points at something that should not be there, so other routes to the same data remain open.

questions.explanation: A boundary check is necessary to close the obvious path and insufficient because it answers only where a path lands, not who may see the record or how else it can be reached. Treating one check as complete coverage is the tempting error.
questions.hint: It answers where a path lands, not who may see the record.

answer.exemplar: A model answer explains that tightening the check closes the direct route through the path field, but the tester can still reach the same records by other routes the check does not govern, such as an export function, a shared folder, an old copy left on a backup, or a reference embedded in a file inside the depot folder. questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a boundary check is necessary but not sufficient
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a boundary check is necessary and what a good test set varies
questions.stem: Explain why a boundary check is necessary but not sufficient, and what a tester should vary when checking it.

answer.exemplar: A model answer explains that the boundary check is necessary because without it any request can name a path outside the intended folder and read material the operator never offered, and it is insufficient because it answers only where a path lands, not who asked or whether the same record is also served by an export, a share or a copy. It adds that a tester who varies only the path field will report a clean result, so a sound test set also varies the route, including the bare parent reference, a differently cased name and a reference held inside the folder that points elsewhere.

questions.explanation: A boundary check closes the obvious route but cannot cover every way the same record is served, so testing must vary the route as well as the input. Assuming the check is complete coverage is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Vary the route, not just the path field.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Two weaknesses used in sequence
questions.learningObjective: State how a pair of logged weaknesses should be recorded
questions.stem: Another team logs a weakness in the crew roster and a weakness in the dispatch console. What should the log say about them?

options.text: That they are duplicates, because both involve the same staff records
options.misconception: assumes shared data means duplicate weaknesses

options.text: That they may be used in sequence, so the pair should be assessed together
That the roster one must be closed first, because the console depends on it
options.misconception: infers a repair order from the listing order

options.text: That the console one is out of scope, since it belongs to another team
options.misconception: dismisses an item because of ownership rather than reach

questions.explanation: Two weaknesses recorded against related services may be used one after another, so the pair should be assessed together rather than as separate items. Treating them as duplicates, as strictly ordered, or as out of scope because of ownership is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Assess them together, not separately.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a published weakness category describes
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a notice whose categories are only partly recognised
questions.stem: A notice lists 9 weaknesses. 3 are in the privilege category, 2 in the availability category, 1 in the information category, and 3 are in no category the depot recognises. What does this support?

options.text: The three unrecognised ones are the most serious, since they are not listed at all
options.misconception: treats an unlisted weakness as automatically the worst

options.text: The notice is unusable, since a category list cannot be applied to any weakness
options.misconception: dismisses the notice wholesale

options.text: Only the three privilege entries need attention, because that category is the priority
options.misconception: assumes one category is always the priority

options.text: A category describes the effect of a weakness, so an unrecognised one needs its effect worked out

questions.explanation: Because a category states the effect of a weakness, an entry in an unfamiliar category still has an effect that the planner must determine before deciding what to do. Assuming unrecognised entries are the worst, or dismissing the notice, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: An unfamiliar category still needs its effect worked out.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Removing a component instead of repairing it
questions.learningObjective: State the status of a weakness closed by component removal
questions.stem: Recently a depot removed an optional module and closed the log entry for that weakness. What is the status of the weakness?

options.text: Closed by removal, since the component that carried it is no longer in the network
Still open, because a weakness stays open until a vendor confirms a fix
options.misconception: assumes a supplier sign-off is always required

options.text: Still open, because removal reduces exposure but never closes the entry
options.misconception: believes removal reduces but never removes exposure

options.text: Closed, but only after the vendor has signed off on the removal
options.misconception: assumes a vendor approval is needed to close an entry

questions.explanation: With the component out of the network there is no remaining path for the weakness, so closing the entry is correct. Assuming a supplier sign-off is always required, or that removal only ever reduces exposure, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything is left to exploit.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Restricting reach while the component stays
questions.learningObjective: Describe how reach has been reduced while a component remains in service
questions.stem: Currently the component stays in the network with a manufacturer repair due in ten weeks. What has the depot done about reach?

options.text: Nothing yet, since reach can only change once the repair arrives
options.misconception: believes reach cannot change before a repair

options.text: Everything, since the component can no longer be reached from other machines
options.misconception: claims the reachable set is already closed off

options.text: Limited the component to the consoles that need it, so the reachable set is smaller
Replaced the component with an identical one, since identical parts behave identically
options.misconception: believes replacing a part changes its exposure

questions.explanation: Restricting the component to the consoles that need it shrinks the reachable set immediately, without waiting for the repair or removing the part. Assuming reach can only change with a repair, or that an identical replacement changes anything, is the tempting error.
questions.hint: Access rules change reach straight away.
